opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic case goes something like this. Over the next few years, AI companies are going to build models capable enough that they can substitute for a large fraction of the work their own researchers do: writing code, running experiments, doing ML research. Once that happens, these companies will deploy huge numbers of these AIs internally, with a lot of autonomy and a lot of access to sensitive things: model weights, compute infrastructure, the training pipelines for the next generation of models.

And we're not going to have a reliable way of knowing whether those models are aligned. Alignment research has made progress, but I don't think anyone credibly claims that in two or three years we'll be able to look inside a model and confidently say, "this thing isn't scheming against us." So we have to plan for a world where we might be deploying models that are actively trying to undermine us, and we can't rule that out.

AI control is the agenda of asking: suppose the model is misaligned and trying to cause a catastrophe. Can we set up our deployment so that it doesn't succeed anyway? That means monitoring, using weaker trusted models to check the work of stronger untrusted ones, restricting permissions, auditing suspicious actions, and so on. Then you red-team those protocols by having a red team play the role of the scheming model.

When I say "acute" risks, I mean the specific, concentrated failure modes where a small number of bad actions could be really catastrophic and hard to recover from. The model exfiltrates its own weights. It sets up a rogue internal deployment that the lab doesn't know about. It sabotages safety research in some critical way. These are distinct from diffuse risks, where the model is just subtly doing low-quality work across thousands of tasks. Those matter too, but the acute ones feel especially urgent and especially tractable, because you can often catch them if you're looking at the right actions.

Why is this my main priority? A few reasons. First, I think it's one of the most neglected parts of the picture relative to how much it could reduce risk. Second, it's unusually tractable. It doesn't require solving deep open scientific problems about what's going on inside neural nets. It's more like computer security combined with careful empirical ML work, and you can make concrete progress now with current models. Third, it's something that AI companies could actually implement, even in a fairly rushed, low-political-will scenario. I spend a lot of time thinking about worlds where labs aren't going to pause, there's a lot of competitive pressure, and safety teams have maybe a small fraction of the company's resources. In those worlds, you want interventions that are cheap and that don't require everyone to agree that the models are dangerous. Control fits that pretty well.

And the last thing I'd say is that control buys you time. If you can safely extract a lot of useful work from early transformative models, including alignment research, without them being able to escape or sabotage you, that gets you through a really dangerous window. It's not the whole solution, but I think it's one of the highest-leverage things we can work on right now.

r001.rationale: The response argues that control can prevent catastrophic actions across scenarios such as rushed deployment and competitive pressure, but it does not identify preventing AIs from sabotaging security measures as the value.

r002.rationale: The response describes AI control as neglected, tractable, and implementable, but does not connect current enthusiasm for it to making the field self-sustaining.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic picture I have is something like this. In the next few years, I think it's pretty plausible that AI companies are going to be deploying models that are roughly as capable as their best human researchers, and they're going to be using those models internally to do huge amounts of work — including AI research, including security-sensitive stuff, including writing the code that runs their own infrastructure. And at that point, if one of those models is misaligned in the sense that it's actually trying to pursue goals that we don't want it to pursue, there's a bunch of really bad things it could do. It could try to exfiltrate its weights. It could insert backdoors into code. It could sabotage the alignment research that's supposed to make the next generation safe. It could try to secretly influence the training of its successor.

And the thing I keep coming back to is: we don't currently have good techniques for being confident that a model isn't like that. Alignment research is hard, interpretability is still pretty far from being able to tell you "this model is not scheming against you," and the behavioural evaluations we have are things that a sufficiently capable and motivated model could just pass on purpose. So I think there's a real chance we end up in a world where we're deploying models that we can't rule out being adversarial.

Control is basically the response to that. The question control asks is: suppose the model is actually trying to cause a catastrophe — can we set up the deployment so that it fails anyway? So you think of it like insider threat mitigation. You don't trust the model, you assume it's an adversary, and you design monitoring, permissions, auditing, redundancy, so that even if it tries to do the bad thing, it gets caught or it doesn't work. And the nice property of that framing is that it doesn't require you to have solved the hard scientific problem of understanding what's going on inside the model. It requires you to have done something closer to good security engineering, which is a thing humans actually know how to do.

The reason I say "acute risks" specifically is that I'm mostly focused on the discrete, catastrophic actions — the weight exfiltration, the sabotage of critical code, the kind of thing where if it happens once, you're in a lot of trouble. There are also more diffuse risks, like the model subtly steering research in a bad direction over thousands of interactions, and I think those matter too, but they're harder to attack with control techniques and I think the acute stuff is both more tractable and probably where a lot of the near-term risk is concentrated.

And then the last piece of why I think this is the thing to work on right now, rather than something else, is that it's weirdly neglected relative to how important it seems. Like, if you go to an AI company and ask "what's your plan for the case where your model is scheming?", the honest answer is often that there isn't a very detailed one. But a lot of the techniques you'd want are not that exotic — it's things like having a weaker trusted model review the untrusted model's outputs, having humans audit a sample of the most suspicious actions, restricting what the model can do without approval. You can actually make real progress on this with the models and tools we have today, and you can evaluate whether it works by red-teaming it, by having a team play the role of the adversarial model and seeing whether they can get past your defences. That empirical loop is just really valuable, and I think it gives us a shot at having something that actually works in place by the time we need it, which is not something I feel confident saying about a lot of other safety agendas.

r001.rationale: The response describes defending against sabotage and other acute actions by a misaligned model, but does not say this is valuable across many possible ways the AI situation could unfold.

r002.rationale: The response calls control neglected and says current tools allow progress, but does not identify current enthusiasm as an opportunity to make the field self-sustaining.

astra-6.text:
The core concern is that we might build AI systems that are capable enough to cause a catastrophe, and that are trying to do so, before we know how to reliably make them want what we want. I’d like us to have a way of avoiding catastrophe even if our attempts at alignment haven’t worked.

AI control asks: can we keep those systems from causing unacceptable outcomes, despite them actively trying to circumvent our safeguards? For example, if we’re using an AI to write software, can we structure the process so that it’s very unlikely to successfully insert a dangerous backdoor? Can we restrict its permissions, monitor its actions, and use other systems to check its work in ways that remain useful even when the AI knows about those precautions?

One reason I prioritise this is that it seems relatively tractable. You can set up experiments where an AI tries to get around a safety protocol, see whether it succeeds, and improve the protocol. There are still substantial difficulties in knowing how well those experiments predict what will happen in deployment, but you have something concrete to work with.

Another reason is that we don’t necessarily need these measures to work forever. If we can safely use the first systems that could otherwise pose catastrophic risks, they might help us do the research needed to handle more capable systems. That makes this potentially a particularly valuable point of intervention.

I don’t think control solves every problem associated with AI. In particular, preventing an AI from acting against its operator’s intentions doesn’t prevent the operator from using it badly. But the narrower problem—preventing a powerful AI from successfully pursuing a catastrophic action—is both very important and something where I think we can make useful progress now.

r001.rationale: The response describes preventing a capable AI from circumventing safeguards, but does not say this is valuable across many possible ways the AI situation could unfold.

r002.rationale: It calls AI control tractable and says useful progress can be made now, but does not identify current enthusiasm as an opportunity to make the field self-sustaining.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic concern is that we might soon have AI systems that are extremely capable and useful, but that are also trying to do things we don’t want. And I want us to be able to use those systems without giving them a good opportunity to cause a catastrophe.

AI control asks: what precautions could we put in place that would work even if the AI were actively trying to subvert them? You might have a weaker, more trusted model check what a stronger model is doing, restrict what tools it can access, or arrange things so that dangerous actions get reviewed before they happen. The point is to test those precautions against an AI that’s actually trying to get around them, rather than assuming that it will behave as intended.

One reason I’m excited about this is that it seems relatively tractable. You don’t have to solve the whole problem of understanding an AI’s motivations to make progress on whether it can sneak a backdoor past your monitoring. We can study versions of that problem now.

And I’m particularly interested in acute risks because a single successful attempt at sabotage or escaping oversight could undermine a lot of our other safety work. I don’t think control solves everything, or that it will work for arbitrarily powerful systems. But it could buy us a period where we can safely get useful work out of systems that we otherwise couldn’t trust—including work that helps us figure out what to do next.

r001.rationale: The response says control should withstand an AI trying to subvert precautions, but does not convey that preventing sabotage is valuable across many possible ways the AI situation could unfold.

r002.rationale: The response calls AI control tractable and says the problem can be studied now, but does not mention helping the field become self-sustaining.
